    Growing globally, staying close to clinicians

    Home/Dental news Eyal Milman has served as CEO of Adin Dental Implant Systems since its founding in 2001. Under his leadership, the company has expanded internationally and now manufactures more than two million implants annually. (All images: Adin Dental Implant Systems)

    Dr Alina Ion, OEMUS MEDIA

    Fri. 27. November 2026

    share save

    Israel-based Adin Dental Implant Systems has been developing and manufacturing dental implant systems for over two decades. The company produces more than two million implants annually and supplies dental professionals in over 80 countries. In this interview, CEO Eyal Milman discusses the scientific evidence behind Adin’s implant systems and its approach to clinical education. He also explains how local partnerships support its international expansion and why he continues to visit clinicians in their practices.

    Mr Milman, could you please introduce Adin’s implant portfolio and explain what guides its development?
    Over the past 25 years, we have built a portfolio that covers routine implant treatment as well as complex rehabilitation. The range includes the UniFit system, which features a conical connection, the 2.75 mm ultra-narrow CloseFit implants and the internal hex systems Touareg, Triple and Swell. We also offer long and zygomatic implants, together with the restorative components and digital solutions that support these treatments.

    Our philosophy is closely connected to the scale of the business. Our manufacturing scale allows us to invest in equipment, testing and research at a level that would be difficult for a smaller operation to sustain. That is one reason we have pursued growth so deliberately.

    We also learn from working in very different markets. That experience informs which products we develop and where we invest next.

    Adin Dental Implant Systems organises more than 900 educational events annually, providing training for clinicians at different stages of their careers. Its international programme covers fundamental implant procedures as well as advanced techniques for full-arch rehabilitation.

    What distinguishes Adin’s implant surface technology?
    Adin’s OsseoFix surface treatment technology uses resorbable calcium phosphate blasting media rather than alumina. Calcium phosphate is biocompatible and similar in composition to the mineral component of natural bone. Its resorbability means that residual blasting material has the potential to be absorbed rather than remain on the implant surface.

    We have investigated the surface through comparative preclinical research. A study published in Clinical Oral Implants Research in 2012 found significantly higher removal torque values for implants treated with resorbable blasting media than for those with an alumina-blasted, acid-etched surface after three weeks in an animal model, indicating stronger early biomechanical fixation.

    Our preclinical work has also included direct comparisons with established implant systems. In a study published in Implant Dentistry in 2013, Adin implants with the OsseoFix surface were evaluated alongside four other commercially available implant systems. The researchers found no statistically significant differences in bone–implant contact between the groups at three or six weeks in an animal model.

    We have now completed another preclinical comparison with the University of Miami, and it is still awaiting publication. Surface research remains an area in which we are investing.

    What published clinical research supports Adin’s implant systems, and how do you plan to expand your international research collaboration?
    A large retrospective study evaluated 3,043 Adin implants in 787 patients and reported an overall survival rate of 98.7% over six to 28 months of follow-up. A separate retrospective study of our tissue-level angled-head system evaluated 185 implants in 29 patients and had a mean follow-up of more than eight years. It reported an overall survival rate of 97.8% and mean marginal bone loss of approximately 0.43 mm at ten years.

    Our preclinical work has involved researchers from New York University in the US, Malmö University in Sweden and Ghent University in Belgium. As we expand, we aim to establish more academic collaborations in the markets where our systems are being used.

    How are clinicians’ evolving needs shaping Adin’s research and development priorities?
    Several years ago, we identified full-arch rehabilitation as an area in which we wanted to invest more heavily. That decision continues to shape our implant range, restorative components and the content of our advanced training courses.

    Our aim is to shorten treatment and chair time, including in cases with limited bone. Supporting immediate loading, where appropriate, and the development of our zygomatic implant range are part of that work. We offer guided surgery solutions and restorative components, including titanium bases, and our implant systems are widely represented in CAD/CAM libraries.

    Adin’s new headquarters and manufacturing facility, currently under construction, will span 38,000 m2. The complex will include approximately 25,000 m2 of production space and is designed to increase the company’s manufacturing capacity to as many as eight million implants annually.

    The pace of adoption differs considerably between markets. Our management and development teams spend time with clinicians and local partners to understand which changes are reaching everyday practice and where further work is needed.

    How does Adin’s international education programme support clinicians at different stages of their careers?
    We organise more than 900 educational events a year and have training centres in countries such as Colombia, India and Israel. The programme ranges from foundational courses to advanced full-arch training and includes webinars, cadaver courses, other practical workshops and clinical training.

    We develop our programmes with local clinical leaders and partners. The subjects clinicians want to study, their experience and the techniques already established in practice differ between countries. Our local teams help determine the programme and remain in contact with participants afterwards.

    What distinguishes Adin in the highly competitive dental implant market?
    For me, the answer is trust: in our products, in our service and in our company being there for the long term. Direct access to the people running the business is part of that.

    I still visit clinicians in their practices when I travel. Our senior team does the same. I want to hear directly what is working, what is difficult and what clinicians need from us. By the time a clinician’s feedback reaches me through several people, a great deal of what the clinician actually said can be lost.

    Being privately owned gives us room to make decisions with those relationships in mind. Many of our managers, engineers and local partners have worked with us for decades. They know one another and know the markets. That continuity has helped us grow while keeping the company accessible to the people using our systems.

    Price is also part of the discussion. We have built the business around affordable quality.

    As Adin expands internationally, which markets are you prioritising, and what guides your approach to establishing a local presence?
    We concentrated for many years on major emerging markets, including India and China, alongside an established presence in European countries such as Italy and Greece. The businesses we built there gave us the financial strength and experience to expand further across Europe and grow our business in the US.

    Europe and the US are now our main expansion priorities. To support this expansion, we are building a new facility that will house our headquarters and substantially increase our manufacturing capacity. In Europe, we are an authorised supplier to Colosseum Dental Group, one of Europe’s largest dental support organisations, and have recently launched a collaboration with Septodont, which is now our exclusive distributor in France.

    Our experience has also made us careful about transferring a business model from one country to another. Argentina and Colombia, for example, have required quite different approaches. We work with local teams to decide how best to develop our business in each market.

    How are Adin and Septodont working together in France, and what does the agreement mean for clinicians there?
    For clinicians in France, the most practical change is local support. Septodont is creating a dedicated implant business unit to provide specialised commercial and clinical support to dental professionals nationwide. French clinicians will have a team they can reach directly, as well as access to local stock and delivery services.

    We also contribute technical expertise and educational programmes, and Septodont brings its local organisation and its long-standing relationships with French dental professionals. Training will be one of our first priorities together. For us, Septodont’s decision to work with Adin is a vote of confidence in the company.

    What role do local partnerships play in Adin’s international strategy, and how do you measure its long-term success?
    Many of our partners have been with us for more than 15 years. They have committed their own resources to building Adin in their countries, and that commitment has to work both ways.

    At the beginning of the pandemic, we told partners to keep cash in their businesses, pay their teams and resume payments to us as they recovered. We gave them that flexibility because we wanted those businesses to survive. We had spent years building them together.

    We operate through distributors in some markets and our own subsidiaries in others. In both cases, building a local business takes sustained investment. The team needs to know that we will stay committed while they develop it.

    Our long-term target is a market share of at least 10% by volume in each market where we operate. We are above that level in some countries.

    Editorial note:

    More information about the company can be found at www.adin-implants.com. This interview was originally published in Issue 4/2026 of implants—international magazine of oral implantology.
